metadata.note: The Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe Railway's Houston-to-transcontinental corridor: built out of Galveston specifically to reach across Texas toward Santa Fe, NM (bypassing Houston), chartered 1873, Santa Fe-controlled from 1887. The Coleman Cutoff (1912-1914) and Lubbock-Texico Cut Off (1912-1914) together completed a direct Houston-to-transcontinental route in March 1914, cutting roughly 500 miles off the old Houston-California routing via Southern Pacific's Sunset Route; the resulting passenger train, eventually named The California Special, is drawn as a separate feature in data/santa_fe_california_special.geojson, layered on top of this layer's track-ownership features. This layer also includes two feeder branches (bonus scope): Fort Worth-Brownwood, which is NOT a Santa Fe property until 1937 -- it was independently built by the Fort Worth and Rio Grande Railway (1891) and then owned by Frisco (1901-1937) before Santa Fe bought and leased it to the GC&SF in 1937 -- and Brownwood-San Angelo, which IS a genuine GC&SF line, built entirely under Santa Fe control from 1888. Sweetwater-Lubbock and Lubbock-Clovis use the same company string and color ('Panhandle and Santa Fe Railway (Santa Fe subsidiary)', #003DA5) as the existing Amarillo-Lubbock feature in data/santa_fe_amarillo_lubbock.geojson so all three group together in the map legend as one company; that existing file's own note explains why its drawn extent (Amarillo-Lubbock only) undersells how long Santa Fe passenger service actually lasted at Lubbock, since it predates this layer.
geometry_sources: Geometry traced from OpenStreetMap via Overpass (overpass-api.de, curl POST), railway=rail/abandoned/disused/razed ways in regional bounding boxes covering each named leg. Ways were assembled into a real-topology graph keyed by OSM node id (nodes within ~11 m / 4 decimal places merged), edges weighted by haversine length times a corridor-distance penalty (quadratic beyond 1.5 km from a polyline through the documented station towns) times an operator weight favoring BNSF/Santa Fe/Panhandle-tagged trackage over crossing lines (Union Pacific, CPKC, Texas & Pacific, Missouri Pacific, Southern Pacific), then routed with Dijkstra between the geocoded (Nominatim, structured city/state/country query) endpoint towns, restricted to the largest connected component. Raw paths were checked for self-intersection/backtracking using cumulative along-path distance (point pairs >=600 m apart along the path whose direct distance is <250 m are flagged); flagged out-and-back yard/dead-end spikes were spliced out, then the result was Douglas-Peucker simplified at 15 m. Final backtrack check: zero flags on every feature below. This is today's BNSF alignment (the corridor is understood to be largely unrelocated since original construction, but no period valuation map was consulted).
Nominatim geocoding (structured city/state/country query, preferring addresstype town/city/village/hamlet over county) for all 52 named station towns on this corridor.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: headway_min is a uniform 1440 (once-daily) guess across every era and every feature in this file -- no era-specific frequency was sourced for any of these track-ownership features (as opposed to the California Special itself, which has real 1954 timetable data in the companion file). avg_speed_kmh values (25-35 km/h) are similarly unsourced guesses. The exact Brownwood-Ballinger mileage on the Brownwood-San Angelo feeder was not found. Bluffdale, TX (the one named stop between Tolar and Stephenville on the Fort Worth-Brownwood feeder) could not be geocoded and is not used as a routing waypoint. Whether any of these corridors have been relocated since original construction was not checked against a period valuation map -- all geometry is today's BNSF alignment. The precise opening date of the Houston-Temple stretch specifically (as opposed to the combined 1886 date used here) was not found.

segments.note: The independent, Galveston-chartered (1873) Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe Railway built this line specifically to reach across Texas toward Santa Fe, NM, bypassing Houston -- Temple was reached by 1886 and Brownwood (via Lampasas) on December 31, 1885. Drawn here as a single 1886 start for the whole Houston-Brownwood core because no more precise per-segment opening date was found for the Houston-Temple stretch; the Temple-Brownwood stretch's own December 31, 1885 opening is documented but the two are combined into one feature/segment per this layer's design. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway signed a stock-acquisition contract with GC&SF March 3, 1886 and had board control by March 23, 1887, ending GC&SF's independent era -- see the Santa Fe-subsidiary feature for 1887 onward. Ends here, not because service ended, but because ownership/control changed.

segments.note: The Coleman Cutoff -- Brownwood, Santa Anna, Coleman, Lawn, Tuscola, Buffalo Gap, View, Sweetwater -- was built by the Santa Fe-controlled GC&SF in 1912-1914 and opened March 1914 (simultaneously with the separately-owned Lubbock-Texico Cut Off, see the Panhandle and Santa Fe features), together completing a direct Houston-to-transcontinental route and cutting roughly 500 miles off the old Houston-California routing via Southern Pacific's Sunset Route. Carried the Houston-Clovis California Special (see the separate named-train layer) from 1915 until its July 1968 discontinuance -- the only documented passenger service on this specific cutoff. End year 1968 reflects passenger discontinuance only; freight is not drawn per this map's passenger-only rule.

segments.note: IMPORTANT CORRECTION vs. this layer's other features: this Fort Worth-Brownwood line is NOT a Gulf, Colorado and Santa Fe property. It was built by the independent Fort Worth and Rio Grande Railway, chartered June 1, 1885, reaching Granbury (40 mi) in October 1887, Comanche by early 1890, and Brownwood (144 mi from Fort Worth) July 1, 1891; the first passenger train ran Fort Worth to Brownwood July 18, 1891. It only becomes part of the Santa Fe system in 1937 (see the later segment on this same geometry) -- see Rule 4 of CLAUDE.md on splitting features at ownership changes. Frisco (the St. Louis-San Francisco Railway) acquired the FW&RG in 1901, ending this independent era -- see the Frisco-era feature for 1901-1937.

segments.note: This is a genuinely GC&SF-built line (unlike the Fort Worth-Brownwood feeder), and it was built entirely under Santa Fe control, so it carries no independent pre-1887 era. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway (operating the GC&SF) opened track from Brownwood to Coleman and Ballinger April 1, 1886 with passenger service from August 1, 1886, then completed a 35-mile extension from Ballinger to San Angelo in 1888, which is when passenger service reached San Angelo -- drawn as the start year here. The route ran via Ballinger, not drawn as a separate named waypoint on this feature but real-traced trackage should pass near it. Named service 'The Angelo' (Dallas/Fort Worth-San Angelo) ran from November 13, 1931; the San Angelo-Brownwood portion of that service was discontinued June 1965 (sources differ by a few weeks on the exact date -- one gives June 1, 1965 for the last train, another June 20, 1965 for the last regularly scheduled train), earlier than the July 1968 end of the connecting California Special and the Fort Worth-Brownwood feeder. Both dates are recorded here rather than silently picking one, per CLAUDE.md Rule 3.
sources: Segment-level: the April 1 1886 Brownwood-Coleman-Ballinger opening and August 1 1886 passenger-service start are from browncountyhistory.org; the 1888 Ballinger-San Angelo extension is from a web search summarizing the TSHA GC&SF handbook entry ('completed a thirty-five mile extension from Ballinger to San Angelo' in 1888); 'The Angelo' train name/1931 start and the June 1965 / June 20 1965 discontinuance dates are from browncountyhistory.org and a San Angelo Live / historicmuralsofsanangelo.org-sourced web search summary. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are unsourced estimates.

properties.geometry_source: Geometry traced from OpenStreetMap via Overpass (overpass-api.de, curl POST), railway=rail/abandoned/disused/razed ways in regional bounding boxes covering each named leg. Ways were assembled into a real-topology graph keyed by OSM node id (nodes within ~11 m / 4 decimal places merged), edges weighted by haversine length times a corridor-distance penalty (quadratic beyond 1.5 km from a polyline through the documented station towns) times an operator weight favoring BNSF/Santa Fe/Panhandle-tagged trackage over crossing lines (Union Pacific, CPKC, Texas & Pacific, Missouri Pacific, Southern Pacific), then routed with Dijkstra between the geocoded (Nominatim, structured city/state/country query) endpoint towns, restricted to the largest connected component. Raw paths were checked for self-intersection/backtracking using cumulative along-path distance (point pairs >=600 m apart along the path whose direct distance is <250 m are flagged); flagged out-and-back yard/dead-end spikes were spliced out, then the result was Douglas-Peucker simplified at 15 m. Final backtrack check: zero flags on every feature below. This is today's BNSF alignment (the corridor is understood to be largely unrelocated since original construction, but no period valuation map was consulted).
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap end to end, no straight-line legs. Traced length 97.99 mi; no independently documented milepost figure for this specific Brownwood-San Angelo stretch was found to compare against (the 1888 Ballinger-San Angelo extension is separately documented as 35 mi, but no source gave a Brownwood-Ballinger figure to add to it). Distance from trace to Brownwood (392 m) and San Angelo (332 m) is well under 500 m at both ends.
